title: The World on Show: Paris, 1889
subtitle: The Exposition Universelle, its tower, its café painters, its foreign music and its living displays, Paris, 1887–1890
intro: On 6 May 1889 President Sadi Carnot opened the Exposition Universelle in Paris, a hundred years after the Estates-General met at Versailles. The fair filled the Champ de Mars, the Trocadéro across the Seine and the Esplanade des Invalides. Its gate was a 300-metre iron tower that Gustave Eiffel's firm had finished on 31 March. Over the next six months the Exposition had about thirty million visits before it closed on 31 October. Some of the strongest impressions it left were not in the official galleries. They were in a Javanese village, a café full of rejected painters, a Russian concert hall and a cowboy arena just outside the gates.

This chapter follows the fair through the people who left a dated record of it. Most of that record is letters and published writing rather than diaries. Edmond de Goncourt kept the one true journal, and he dined on the tower in July. The van Gogh family wrote letters between Paris and the asylum at Saint-Rémy. Gauguin wrote letters and a newspaper article from Brittany. The musicologist Julien Tiersot published his notes on the music within the year. Debussy's famous encounter with the gamelan, on the other hand, is known only from what he and a friend wrote years later, and it is marked that way here.

The tower itself had begun as a quarrel. In February 1887 writers and artists, Maupassant and Gounod among them, signed a protest in Le Temps against it, and Eiffel answered in the same paper. By September 1889 Gounod was lunching on the first platform with Eiffel and Thomas Edison, and Edison was writing Eiffel a dedication in praise of engineering. The Galerie des Machines beside it held Edison's phonographs. Elsewhere on the grounds, much less noticed, stood a Benz motor car.

The fair also put living people on show. About sixty Javanese and Sundanese lived in a kampong built for the Dutch section, and they danced and played the gamelan every day. On the Esplanade des Invalides the French Ministry of the Colonies built villages for people from New Caledonia, Senegal, the Sudan, Gabon and Indochina. Outside the gates, Buffalo Bill's Wild West brought about a hundred Lakota performers to Neuilly. These people appear almost entirely in other people's records: newspapers, engravings, photographs and the notes of visitors. The chapter says so plainly. It gives the few names that survive, such as the dancers Wakiem, Sariem, Soekia and Taminah and the Lakota leader Red Shirt, and it reports what was printed about them without repeating the visitors' gaze.

Read side by side, the eyes show one fair seen in very different ways. To Eiffel it was a triumph of building, and Maupassant fled from it. Theo van Gogh found its pictures weak. Rimsky-Korsakov played to thin houses. Debussy heard in the kampong a music that he said later made Western harmony look like a ghost. The people in the villages went home by train and steamer, and only a Javanese court record made forty years later tells something of the journey in their own language.
calendar_note: All dates are in the Gregorian calendar. The Exposition officially closed on 31 October 1889, though some sources give an extended closing in early November. Press items are dated by issue, and the illustrated weeklies came out on Saturdays. Several letters, including Vincent van Gogh's from Saint-Rémy and Gauguin's to Bernard, are undated in the original and are placed by their editors; these are marked approx. Reports about the Javanese performers' journeys come from Dutch-Indies newspapers and carry those papers' dates.

eyes.name: Gustave Eiffel
eyes.role: Engineer and contractor, aged 56 in 1889; his firm designed and built the 300-metre tower that served as the Exposition's entrance arch
eyes.where: The Champ de Mars building site and, from 1889, his private rooms near the top of the tower
eyes.form: published reply, speech (reported), dedications and later documents
eyes.authenticity: His reply to the 1887 protest was printed in Le Temps; his speech of 31 March 1889 survives in press reports, not as a manuscript diary. The dedication Edison wrote for him in September 1889 is held with the tower's archives and widely reproduced.
eyes.bio: Eiffel had built bridges and viaducts and the iron frame of the Statue of Liberty before the tower. He answered the artists' protest in print, climbed the unfinished stairs to raise the flag in March 1889, and kept rooms at the top where he received guests. His record is public and official rather than private.

sources.title: Lettres volées: Dossier Tour Eiffel (protest of 1887, Eiffel's reply, Goncourt, Gauguin, Maupassant)
HISTORY.com: Eiffel Tower opens (31 March 1889)
Tour Eiffel: Thanks to the phonograph, Gustave Eiffel's voice travels through the ages

eyes.name: Guy de Maupassant
eyes.role: Novelist and story writer, aged 36 when he signed the 1887 protest; 39 in 1889
eyes.where: Paris; in 1889–90 travelling away from Paris, partly on the Mediterranean
eyes.authenticity: The protest appeared in Le Temps on 14 February 1887 over many signatures. La Vie errante (1890) is a crafted travel book, not a diary; its opening chapter, 'Lassitude', is his account of leaving Paris and the tower behind.
eyes.bio: Maupassant was among the writers who put their names to the protest. Three years later he opened a travel book by saying that the tower, visible from everywhere, had helped drive him out of Paris and out of France. He is the chapter's voice of refusal.

sources.title: Lettres volées: Dossier Tour Eiffel (protest of 1887, Eiffel's reply, Goncourt, Gauguin, Maupassant)

eyes.name: Edmond de Goncourt
eyes.role: Novelist, collector of Japanese art and diarist, aged 67; kept the Journal alone since his brother Jules's death in 1870
eyes.side: The literary Paris of Zola, Daudet and Charpentier
eyes.where: His house at Auteuil and the Paris dinner tables he recorded
eyes.vantage_label: diarist on the tower's first platform
eyes.authenticity: The Journal des Goncourt was published by Edmond himself in a revised selection from 1887; the volume covering 1889 appeared in 1894. The full text was published only from 1956. The printed entries are revised by their author.
eyes.bio: Goncourt was the one true diarist in this chapter. He had collected Japanese prints since the 1860s and watched the Paris art world closely. In July 1889 he dined on the tower with Zola and his publisher and wrote down the ride and the view.

sources.title: Lettres volées: Dossier Tour Eiffel (protest of 1887, Eiffel's reply, Goncourt, Gauguin, Maupassant)
Wikisource: Journal des Goncourt, VIII, année 1889

eyes.name: Paul Gauguin
eyes.role: Painter, aged 41; organiser of the 'Impressionist and Synthetist' group show at the Café des Arts
eyes.side: The Pont-Aven painters around Gauguin and Émile Bernard
eyes.where: Paris in spring 1889; from early June at Pont-Aven and Le Pouldu, Brittany
eyes.vantage_label: exhibitor on the fringe of the fair
eyes.authenticity: His letters to Bernard, Schuffenecker and Theo van Gogh were edited by Malingue (1946) and Merlhès (1984); many are undated and editors' placements differ. His 'Notes sur l'art à l'Exposition universelle' appeared in Le Moderniste illustré in July 1889.
eyes.bio: Gauguin could not get into the official art sections, so he and his friends hung their pictures in a café inside the grounds. He also walked the Exposition as a critic, praising the iron buildings and visiting the Javanese village. His later borrowings from Javanese and other non-European art begin, by most accounts, in these months.

sources.title: The Volpini Exhibition, 1889
NGA: Poster for the Exposition de peintures du groupe impressionniste et synthétiste, Café des Arts
Lettres volées: Dossier Tour Eiffel (protest of 1887, Eiffel's reply, Goncourt, Gauguin, Maupassant)

eyes.name: Vincent van Gogh
eyes.role: Painter, aged 36; a voluntary patient at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole from 8 May 1889
eyes.where: Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, about 700 km from the fair, which he never saw
eyes.authenticity: The letters were first published by Jo van Gogh-Bonger in 1914 and are now edited in full by the Van Gogh Museum and Huygens ING (2009). Many Saint-Rémy letters are undated and dated by editors from their contents.
eyes.bio: Vincent followed the Exposition through Theo's letters and the newspapers. He wished he could see Charles Garnier's houses of all nations, and he was sceptical of Gauguin's café show. His distance makes him a measure of how the fair looked from outside Paris.

sources.title: Vincent van Gogh to Theo, Saint-Rémy, c. 9 June 1889 (letter 594)

eyes.name: Theo van Gogh
eyes.role: Art dealer, aged 32, manager of the Boulevard Montmartre branch of Boussod, Valadon et Cie; married Jo Bonger on 17 April 1889
eyes.side: The van Gogh brothers; the Paris dealers
eyes.where: Paris, cité Pigalle and the Boulevard Montmartre gallery
eyes.authenticity: Theo's letters to Vincent survive in the Van Gogh Museum and are published in the complete edition (2009) and in older English translations.
eyes.bio: Theo saw the Exposition's picture galleries, the café show and the painters themselves. He turned down Gauguin's request to hang Vincent's work at the café and reported both sides to his brother. His letters give the dealer's view of the fair.

sources.title: Theo van Gogh to Vincent, 22 May 1889 (letter T09)
Theo van Gogh to Vincent, 16 June 1889 (letter T10)
Theo van Gogh to Vincent, 16 July 1889 (letter T12)

eyes.name: Johanna van Gogh-Bonger
eyes.role: Theo's wife of three weeks in May 1889, aged 26; later the editor of the van Gogh letters
eyes.vantage_label: newcomer to Paris on opening day
eyes.authenticity: Her letters to Vincent are in the Van Gogh Museum and are included in the complete edition of the correspondence.
eyes.bio: Jo had just moved to Paris from Amsterdam when the fair opened. Her letter of 8 May records the city stopping for the opening rather than the opening itself. She later published the letters that made Vincent famous.

sources.title: Jo van Gogh-Bonger to Vincent, 8 May 1889 (letter T08)

eyes.name: Claude Debussy
eyes.role: Composer, aged 26; a recent Prix de Rome winner back from the Villa Medici
eyes.where: Paris; the Javanese kampong on the Exposition grounds
eyes.authenticity: No diary or letter of 1889 records his visits. The evidence is his letter to Pierre Louÿs of 22 January 1895, his article of 1913, and Robert Godet's recollection published in La Revue musicale in May 1926. All are later than the event.
eyes.bio: Debussy is now the best-known listener to the Javanese musicians. He spoke of the gamelan for years afterwards. The story of his hours in the kampong rests on later memory, his own and his friend Godet's.

sources.title: Richard Mueller, 'Javanese Influence on Debussy's Fantaisie and Beyond' (PDF)

eyes.name: Julien Tiersot
eyes.role: Musicologist and composer, aged 32; assistant librarian at the Paris Conservatoire
eyes.where: The Exposition's music venues, especially the Javanese kampong
eyes.authenticity: His observations were published in 1889 as Promenades musicales à l'Exposition and collected in Musiques pittoresques (Paris, 1889). They are journalism written during or just after the fair, not a diary.
eyes.bio: Tiersot went back to the kampong again and again and tried to write the music down in Western notation. He compared the dancers to figures from French opera and fiction. He also named a few of the performers, which few other visitors did.

sources.title: Julien Tiersot (biography)
Richard Mueller, 'Javanese Influence on Debussy's Fantaisie and Beyond' (PDF)

eyes.name: The performers of the Javanese kampong
eyes.role: About sixty people from Java, most of them Sundanese from West Java and about ten from Central Java (Solo and Yogyakarta). They included four young dancers named in the press as Wakiem, Sariem, Soekia and Taminah, aged about 12 to 16, and musicians, craftsmen and builders
eyes.side: Javanese and Sundanese subjects of the Netherlands East Indies, brought by a private Dutch committee
eyes.where: The kampong ('village') on the Exposition grounds, Champ de Mars

waypoints.label: Parakan Salak and Sukabumi, West Java

eyes.form: records made by others (press, books, photographs); one later Javanese account
eyes.language: Javanese, Sundanese and Malay; recorded in French and Dutch
eyes.authenticity: The performers left no diaries or letters known today. Almost everything about them was written by European visitors, organisers and newspapers. Names and roles differ between sources: the press called the dancers court dancers of the Mangkunegaran, while a Java newspaper said they were a troupe hired in Solo. A Javanese-language account kept at the Mangkunegaran court (1929) draws on participants' memories.
eyes.bio: The kampong was one of the most visited sights of the fair, and its music is the reason Debussy's name is tied to it. The people themselves appear mostly as subjects of other people's descriptions. This chapter gives the names and facts that survive and leaves out the visitors' commentary on their bodies.

sources.title: Southeast Asian Studies (Kyoto) 36:4 — study of the Javanese kampong at the 1889 Exposition
Richard Mueller, 'Javanese Influence on Debussy's Fantaisie and Beyond' (PDF)

eyes.name: The people of the colonial villages
eyes.role: Men, women and children from French colonies, among them Kanak from New Caledonia, Senegalese and Sudanese from West Africa, people from Gabon and Congo, and Annamese and Tonkinese from Indochina. Some came as soldiers, actors or artisans
eyes.side: Colonial subjects of France, displayed by the Ministry of the Colonies
eyes.where: The colonial section on the Esplanade des Invalides
eyes.form: records made by others (illustrated press, photographs, official guides)
eyes.authenticity: No first-person record from these villages is known for 1889. Illustrated weeklies and photographers recorded them under group labels such as 'Canaques' or 'Sénégalais', and individual names are almost never given. Dates here are the issue dates of those publications.
eyes.bio: The colonial section was designed to show the empire as orderly and profitable, a century after 1789. The people who lived in its villages for six months are visible only through others' images and captions. This chapter records what was printed and when, and says plainly that their own words are missing.

sources.title: Human Zoos archive: 1889 Exposition Universelle image gallery (press captions)
Bridgeman Images: Tinayre, 'Exposition universelle 1889, le village canaque à l'esplanade des Invalides' (engraving)

eyes.name: Buffalo Bill's Wild West (William F. Cody, Annie Oakley and company)
eyes.role: Touring show of about 218 people, including about 100 Lakota Sioux led by Red Shirt, cowboys, Mexican vaqueros and the sharpshooters Annie Oakley (aged 29) and Lillian Smith
eyes.side: American show business; the Lakota performers under contract
eyes.where: A rented arena at Neuilly, outside the Exposition grounds
eyes.form: newspaper reports and programmes; later memoirs
eyes.authenticity: The company's time in Paris is known from American and French newspapers, the 1889 French-language programme and later memoirs (Cody's and Oakley's autobiographies). The Lakota performers' own words from 1889 are scarce; they appear mainly in others' reports.
eyes.bio: The Wild West was not part of the Exposition, but it drew Exposition crowds twice a day. The President of the Republic came, and the painter Rosa Bonheur spent days at the camp. Like the colonial villages, it put living people on show, though as paid performers who also toured.

sources.title: Cody Archive: 'The Wild West on the Sea', Omaha Daily Bee, 12 May 1889 (from the New York Herald)
BnF / CNAC Cirque: Buffalo Bill and the Wild West Show
Popular Science: In 1889, Paris became obsessed with the Wild West
Cody Archive: 1889 Buffalo Bill's Wild West programme in French

eyes.name: Thomas Alva Edison
eyes.role: American inventor, aged 42; his phonographs and electric lighting filled a large display in the Galerie des Machines
eyes.where: Paris, August–September 1889, with his wife Mina
eyes.authenticity: The trip is documented in the Edison Papers (Rutgers), contemporary newspapers and the dedication he wrote for Eiffel. He did not keep a diary on this trip.
eyes.bio: Edison arrived as the most famous inventor in the world. In Paris he was fêted by engineers, scientists and the government. His lunch on the tower with Eiffel and Gounod brought together the builder and one of the tower's old opponents.

sources.title: Edison Tinfoil: Edison at the Eiffel Tower, 10 September 1889
Tour Eiffel: Thanks to the phonograph, Gustave Eiffel's voice travels through the ages

eyes.name: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
eyes.role: Composer and naval officer turned professor at the St Petersburg Conservatory, aged 45
eyes.side: The Belyayev circle of Russian composers
eyes.where: The Trocadéro concert hall, across the Seine from the tower
eyes.authenticity: His account is in Chronicle of My Musical Life, written between 1876 and 1906 and published in 1909. The concert programmes are documented independently.
eyes.bio: Rimsky-Korsakov conducted two concerts of Russian music in the Exposition's Trocadéro hall, paid for by the publisher Mitrofan Belyayev. He remembered small audiences. Young French musicians in the hall, among them the teenage Ravel and Ricardo Viñes, are said to have been struck by what they heard.

sources.title: Russian Symphony Concerts (programmes of 22 and 29 June 1889)

entries.headline: Writers and artists protest the 'useless and monstrous' tower
entries.digest: Le Temps printed an open letter to Adolphe Alphand, director of the Exposition's works, from writers, painters, sculptors and architects. They called the planned tower useless and monstrous and asked him to defend the beauty of Paris against it. Maupassant's name was on it with those of Gounod, Garnier, Dumas fils, Coppée, Leconte de Lisle, Sully Prudhomme and Meissonier, among others. Construction had begun on 28 January.
entries.source_note: Le Temps, 14 Feb 1887, as summarised in the Lettres volées dossier (which notes that Zola and Huysmans did not sign, contrary to some websites). Signatory names from standard accounts.

entries.headline: Eiffel replies: judge the tower when it stands
entries.digest: Eiffel answered in the same paper. He said the protest came too late and that nobody could judge a tower that had not yet been built. He argued that engineering could produce its own beauty and that the tower would serve science and national defence. Alphand also replied that the tower would be the centrepiece of the fair.
entries.source_note: Eiffel's interview in Le Temps, 14 Feb 1887, and Alphand's reply, summarised in the Lettres volées dossier.

entries.place: Summit of the tower, Champ de Mars
entries.headline: Eiffel climbs the stairs and raises the flag
entries.digest: The lifts were not finished, so Eiffel and a few companions climbed the stairs to the top. He raised a large tricolour, and fireworks went off from the second platform. Prime Minister Pierre Tirard and other officials waited lower down. Back on the ground Eiffel spoke to the guests and to about two hundred of the workers who had built the tower in just over two years.
entries.source_note: HISTORY.com 'Eiffel Tower opens'; press accounts of the ceremony. The text of the speech is known from newspaper reports.

entries.headline: The first Javanese arrive to build the kampong
entries.digest: Dutch newspapers reported that forty-three Javanese had arrived for the Exposition. More followed, and by the summer the village held about sixty people, roughly forty men and twenty women. Most were Sundanese from West Java, recruited through tea planters near Sukabumi. They spoke Javanese, Sundanese and Malay and did not always understand each other.
entries.source_note: Dutch press reports as summarised in the Southeast Asian Studies (Kyoto) 36:4 article on the kampong; the arrival date comes from a report published later in May.

entries.headline: The Wild West sails for France in the rain
entries.digest: The steamer Persian Monarch left New York for Le Havre in cold, steady rain. On board were 218 people, among them about a hundred Sioux performers, thirty-two cowboys, seven Mexican vaqueros, and Annie Oakley and Lillian Smith as the women sharpshooters. Horses, buffalo and dogs went too. The plan was several months in Paris, then the rest of the Continent.
entries.quote: The Wild West on the Sea
entries.source_note: 'The Wild West on the Sea', Omaha Daily Bee, 12 May 1889, reprinted from the New York Herald (Cody Archive).

entries.headline: Gauguin urges Bernard to see the Javanese dances
entries.digest: In a letter to Émile Bernard, Gauguin told him he had missed something by not coming to the Javanese village. He described the dances there as Hindu dances and said all the art of India could be seen in them. He mentioned collecting photographs of Cambodian art as well. The letter has no date in the original.
entries.source_note: Gauguin to Bernard, published in Malingue's edition of the letters (1946); widely cited in Gauguin studies. Date and wording not checked against the manuscript.

entries.headline: The Exposition opens under the tower
entries.digest: President Sadi Carnot opened the Exposition Universelle on the centenary of the meeting of the Estates-General of 1789. The tower stood at the entrance to the Champ de Mars, with the Galerie des Machines and the Palais des Beaux-Arts beyond it. Many sections and the tower's lifts were still unfinished. Several monarchies sent no official delegation to a fair that celebrated the Revolution.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts of the opening; NGA slideshow 'Exposition Universelle de 1889'.

entries.headline: Jo stays home while Paris opens its fair
entries.digest: Jo told Vincent that the exhibition had opened on Monday and that the art shops had closed for the day. She and Theo did not go. They spent the day at home instead. She had been in Paris less than three weeks.
entries.source_note: Jo van Gogh-Bonger to Vincent, Paris, 8 May 1889 (webexhibits T08).

entries.headline: The tower opens to the paying public
entries.digest: Visitors were admitted to the tower, but at first they had to climb the stairs because the lifts were still being finished. The lifts to the upper levels came into service later in the season. By the end of 1889 nearly two million people had gone up.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts of the tower's opening; visitor total from tower histories, not checked against the 1889 ledgers.

entries.headline: The Wild West opens at Neuilly
entries.digest: After a week of building on rented land at Neuilly, the company opened its arena outside the Exposition grounds. President Carnot and his wife were among an audience of thousands. Annie Oakley skipped into the ring and shot glass balls thrown into the air, dropping each empty gun for another. The Paris Herald reported a great success the next morning.
entries.source_note: BnF/CNAC Cirque page; Popular Science (2023). The exact opening date is from secondary accounts and was not checked against the Paris press.

entries.headline: Theo finds the fair's pictures weak
entries.digest: Theo told Vincent that the paintings at the Universal Exhibition and the Salon were weak. The Dutch school looked good beside the rest, he thought. He had seen Gauguin, who was now making sculpture and would soon go to Pont-Aven. He asked which of Vincent's canvases should go to the Indépendants.
entries.source_note: Theo van Gogh to Vincent, Paris, 22 May 1889 (webexhibits T09).

entries.place: Café des Arts, Champ de Mars
entries.headline: The 'Impressionist and Synthetist' show opens in a café
entries.digest: Gauguin, Schuffenecker, Bernard, Laval, Anquetin, Louis Roy, Fauché and Daniel de Monfreid hung about ninety-four works in Monsieur Volpini's Grand Café des Arts, opposite the Press Pavilion. Gauguin showed seventeen works and a folio of eleven zincographs on yellow paper. The press mostly ignored the show and almost nothing sold. By the time it opened Gauguin had gone back to Brittany.
entries.source_note: Wikipedia 'The Volpini Exhibition, 1889'; Musée de Pont-Aven story on Google Arts & Culture; NGA poster record. Exact opening day not established.

entries.headline: Vincent wishes he could see the houses of all nations
entries.digest: Vincent wrote that he would have liked to see the Egyptian house in the history of human dwellings built at the exhibition. He named the architect as Jules Garnier; it was in fact Charles Garnier, one of the signatories of the protest against the tower. He had seen an announcement of a show by Gauguin, Bernard, Anquetin and others. He doubted that a new group would be any wiser than the old ones and called the quarrels storms in a teacup.
entries.source_note: Vincent to Theo, Saint-Rémy, c. 9 June 1889 (webexhibits 594); date is the editors'.

entries.headline: Theo keeps Vincent's pictures out of the café
entries.digest: Theo told Vincent that Gauguin and his friends were showing at a café on the grounds. He had first meant to include Vincent's work but had been put off by the group's manner. Going there felt to him like entering the Universal Exhibition by the back stairs. Gauguin had left for Pont-Aven two weeks earlier.
entries.source_note: Theo van Gogh to Vincent, Paris, 16 June 1889 (webexhibits T10).

entries.headline: First Russian concert at the Trocadéro
entries.digest: Rimsky-Korsakov conducted the Colonne orchestra in Glinka, Borodin's In the Steppes of Central Asia, the first movement of Tchaikovsky's First Piano Concerto, his own Second Symphony ('Antar'), Balakirev, Cui, Lyadov, Dargomyzhsky and Glazunov's Stenka Razin. The Russian publisher Belyayev paid for the series. The hall was large and the music almost unknown in Paris.
entries.source_note: Programme as given in 'Russian Symphony Concerts' (citing Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, pp. 301–02).

entries.headline: The young dancers become a picture-paper subject
entries.digest: Le Journal illustré published an image of the 'little dancers' of the Javanese kampong. By now crowds came each day to watch the dancers and hear the gamelan. The dancers' names, Wakiem, Sariem, Soekia and Taminah, were printed in varying spellings. Their status was disputed: the organisers called them court dancers of the Mangkunegaran, but a Java newspaper later said they were a troupe hired in Solo.
entries.source_note: Caption 'Les petites danseuses du Kampong Javanais', Le Journal illustré, 23 June 1889 (Human Zoos archive); names and dispute from the Kyoto SEAS 36:4 article.

entries.headline: Second concert, and an empty-feeling hall
entries.digest: The second programme brought Glazunov's Second Symphony, Rimsky-Korsakov's Piano Concerto, Glinka's Kamarinskaya, Borodin's Polovtsian Dances, Musorgsky's Night on Bald Mountain and the Capriccio espagnol. Rimsky-Korsakov later remembered thin audiences and blamed Belyayev's dislike of advertising. Ravel and Viñes, then teenagers, are said to have taken away a piano-duet score of Antar.
entries.source_note: 'Russian Symphony Concerts' (citing My Musical Life, pp. 301–02, written later). The Ravel–Viñes detail rests on later recollection.

entries.headline: Debussy spends hours with the gamelan
entries.digest: Debussy, back in Paris from the Villa Medici, went to the kampong many times. His friend Robert Godet later remembered him listening for hours to the gamelan and watching the dancers. No letter from 1889 records his visits. What the Javanese music meant to him is known from what he wrote afterwards.
entries.source_note: Robert Godet, 'En marge de la marge', La Revue musicale, May 1926, as cited by Mueller.

entries.headline: Tiersot tries to write the gamelan down
entries.digest: Tiersot visited the kampong again and again and transcribed melodies in Western notation. He described the gamelan, the dances and a procession with eight angklung and a drum. He named a dancer, Tamina, and a performer, Rimbo. He compared the dancers to Flaubert's Salammbô and to Pamina in The Magic Flute. He judged the gamelan the Dutch had given the Conservatoire in 1887 to be a silent object by comparison.
entries.source_note: Tiersot, Musiques pittoresques: promenades musicales à l'Exposition de 1889 (Paris, 1889), pp. 31–47, as summarised by Mueller and the Kyoto SEAS article.

entries.place: First platform of the Eiffel Tower
entries.headline: Goncourt dines on the tower with Zola
entries.digest: Goncourt went up the tower with his publisher Georges Charpentier, Zola, Abel Hermant and Armand Dayot and dined on the first platform. He wrote down the lift ride, which he compared to a ship putting out to sea. He described the sunset over Paris and the walk down the iron stairs, like climbing down a ship's rigging. Zola had not signed the protest of 1887.
entries.source_note: Journal des Goncourt, 2 July 1889, as excerpted in the Lettres volées dossier.

entries.headline: Gauguin praises the iron buildings
entries.digest: Le Moderniste illustré printed the first part of Gauguin's 'Notes on art at the Universal Exhibition', with the second a week later. He praised the iron architecture of the Exposition and its engineers. The tower, he suggested, hinted at a new decorative art of iron lacework. The artist shut out of the official galleries wrote as a critic of the whole fair.
entries.source_note: Le Moderniste illustré, 4 and 11 July 1889, as summarised in the Lettres volées dossier.

entries.headline: Theo sends Vincent Gauguin's article
entries.digest: Theo said Gauguin was writing for a paper and that he was sending it to Vincent. Gauguin had written the week before asking for Vincent's address, which he had lost. Jacob Meyer de Haan, now painting beside Gauguin in Brittany, reported that he was doing very fine work.
entries.source_note: Theo van Gogh to Vincent, Paris, 16 July 1889 (webexhibits T12).

entries.headline: A Paris paper praises 'Miss Oackley's' rifle
entries.digest: La Journée parisienne praised the shooting of Annie Oakley, spelling her name 'Oackley'. Each of the two daily shows drew about fifteen thousand people, many of them Exposition visitors who took the omnibus out to Neuilly. Red Shirt led the Lakota performers in the arena and their camp was open to visitors.
entries.source_note: La Journée parisienne, 20 July 1889, as cited on the BnF/CNAC Cirque page.

entries.headline: Rosa Bonheur paints Buffalo Bill
entries.digest: The painter Rosa Bonheur, then sixty-seven, made repeated visits to the camp and sketched the Lakota performers, the horses and the buffalo. She painted Cody on his white horse, a portrait he sent home to his family. Her sketches are among the few close records of the Lakota in Paris, though they were seen through her eyes, not theirs.
entries.source_note: BnF/CNAC Cirque page; Popular Science (2023). Visit dates not established.

entries.headline: Edison arrives to see his own exhibit
entries.digest: Edison and his wife Mina arrived in Paris for the fair, where his company's display of phonographs and electric lamps took up a large space in the Galerie des Machines. Crowds queued to hear the talking machines through ear tubes. He was received by scientists and officials and made a commander of the Legion of Honour.
entries.source_note: Edison Papers listings for August 1889 (Rutgers); edisontinfoil.com. Arrival day and honour date not checked against the documents.

entries.headline: The picture press shows Annamese soldiers at a meal
entries.digest: L'Illustration printed an engraving of Annamese tirailleurs, colonial soldiers from Indochina, eating together. The Annamese theatre in the colonial section was one of its most visited attractions. The soldiers and actors are labelled by group, not by name. No account in their own words is known.
entries.source_note: Caption 'Le Repas des Tirailleurs Annamites', L'Illustration, 24 Aug 1889 (Human Zoos archive).

entries.headline: The Kanak village appears in L'Illustration
entries.digest: L'Illustration published an engraving of the 'village canaque' on the Esplanade des Invalides, the dwellings of people brought from New Caledonia, a French penal and settler colony. The caption names the place and the group but none of the people. Within the empire, New Caledonia's Kanak had risen against the colonists in 1878.
entries.source_note: Caption 'Village Canaque', L'Illustration, 31 Aug 1889 (Human Zoos archive); Tinayre engraving (Bridgeman).

entries.place: First platform and summit of the tower
entries.headline: Lunch on the tower with Eiffel and Gounod
entries.digest: Edison lunched at the Brébant restaurant on the tower's first platform with Eiffel, a party of engineers and the composer Charles Gounod. Edison, Eiffel and Gounod all signed a place card for one of the guests. The party then went up to Eiffel's private rooms near the top, where Edison gave him a new phonograph. Gounod had signed the protest against the tower in 1887.
entries.source_note: edisontinfoil.com; Tour Eiffel official site on Edison's visit.

entries.place: Eiffel's rooms at the top of the tower
entries.headline: Eiffel receives a phonograph and a dedication
entries.digest: Edison gave Eiffel the newest model phonograph and wrote him a dedication in English. It praised Eiffel as the builder of a gigantic work of modern engineering and saluted all engineers, including God, whom he called the Great Engineer. Two years later Eiffel recorded his own voice on wax cylinders that the Bibliothèque nationale still holds.
entries.quote: the brave builder of so gigantic and original specimen of modern Engineering
entries.source_note: Tour Eiffel official site, 'Thanks to the phonograph, Gustave Eiffel's voice travels through the ages'.

entries.headline: The Senegalese village in the illustrated press
entries.digest: L'Illustration published an image of the Senegalese village, where families lived and worked in front of visitors for the season. Other villages represented Gabon and Congo, Tonkin and the Sudan. The official guides and the press described these displays as lessons in colonial progress. The individuals in them are seldom named.
entries.source_note: Caption 'Village Sénégalais', L'Illustration, 21 Sept 1889 (Human Zoos archive).

entries.headline: The Exposition closes
entries.digest: The Exposition officially closed after almost six months and some thirty million visits. The tower had been built for twenty years and was meant to come down in 1909. Its use for radio and science later saved it. Some sources give an extended closing in early November.
entries.source_note: Standard accounts; NGA slideshow gives 6 May–6 November 1889. Visitor total from secondary sources.

entries.headline: Fifty-four Javanese leave Paris on the morning express
entries.digest: Java newspapers reported that fifty-four people from the kampong left Paris on the eleven o'clock express. They went by train to Genoa and sailed for Java. Five others had already left early because of illness in their families. The groups split on arrival for Bandung, the tea estates, and Solo and Yogyakarta.
entries.source_note: De Locomotief, 23 and 26 Nov 1889, and other Dutch-Indies papers as summarised in the Kyoto SEAS 36:4 article.

entries.headline: 'Les Soudanais' in Le Monde illustré
entries.digest: As the fair ended, Le Monde illustré printed an image of the 'Soudanais', people from the French Sudan who had been displayed in the colonial section. The people in the colonial villages went home or moved on to other shows. Where most of them went is not recorded.
entries.source_note: Caption 'Les Soudanais', Le Monde illustré, 9 Nov 1889 (Human Zoos archive).

entries.headline: Home in Solo with Eiffel Tower medals
entries.digest: A newspaper in the Indies reported that the people from Solo had come home in good spirits, wearing Eiffel Tower medals. Days later another paper complained that one dancer's father had lived off his daughter's earnings. These reports are among the last printed traces of the kampong's people.
entries.source_note: Reports dated 4 and 10 Dec 1889 in Dutch-Indies papers, as summarised in the Kyoto SEAS 36:4 article.

entries.headline: Maupassant says the tower drove him away
entries.digest: Maupassant opened his travel book La Vie errante with a chapter called 'Lassitude'. He wrote that he had left Paris and even France because the tower was visible from everywhere and he had grown tired of it. He also mocked the claim that it stood for a new architecture. The book appeared in 1890, the year after the fair.
entries.source_note: Maupassant, La Vie errante (Paris, 1890), chapter 'Lassitude', as summarised in the Lettres volées dossier.

entries.headline: Debussy to Louÿs: remember the Javanese music
entries.digest: Writing to his friend Pierre Louÿs, Debussy recalled the Javanese music of 1889. He said it could express every shade of meaning, and that beside it the tonic and dominant of Western harmony seemed like ghosts. It is his earliest known written reference to the gamelan, more than five years after he heard it.
entries.source_note: Debussy to Pierre Louÿs, 22 Jan 1895 (Lesure ed.), as cited by Mueller.

entries.headline: Debussy's essay on taste praises Javanese counterpoint
entries.digest: In an essay on taste published in the S.I.M. review, Debussy wrote that Javanese music had a counterpoint that made Palestrina's seem like child's play. He compared Western percussion to the noise of a country fair. He reminded readers of the Javanese musicians at the 1889 fair, twenty-four years earlier. The essay appeared a few months before the premiere of The Rite of Spring.
entries.source_note: Debussy, 'Du goût', S.I.M. Revue musicale, 1913, as cited by Mueller; exact issue date not checked.

entries.headline: A Javanese account of the journey to Paris
entries.digest: A Javanese-language record kept at the Mangkunegaran court in Solo described the departure for Paris and listed who had gone. It named a man and two women dancers from Solo, a batik worker from Yogyakarta, a kris-maker, people from the Tengger highlands, and others from Bandung and Batavia. Drawn from participants' memories forty years on, it is the nearest surviving thing to the performers' own account.
entries.source_note: Mangkunegaran record (1929), as described in the Kyoto SEAS 36:4 article; not seen directly.

convergences.label: The protest and the reply
convergences.note: On the same day the same paper printed both sides. The writers spoke for an old idea of Paris. Eiffel answered that nobody could judge a building that did not yet exist, and he bet on the tower being seen before it was judged.

convergences.label: Opening week
convergences.note: Eiffel's tower became the gate to the fair, and Jo stayed at home while the shops shut. The Javanese had been building their village for a month. The Wild West was at sea, a few days from Le Havre.

convergences.label: The café show, seen from three places
convergences.note: Gauguin hung his group's work in a café and left for Brittany. Theo, in Paris, kept Vincent's pictures out of it and found the place shabby. Vincent, in Saint-Rémy, had only an announcement and thought the whole quarrel trivial.

convergences.label: A week of foreign music
convergences.note: Rimsky-Korsakov's Russian concerts at the Trocadéro and the gamelan in the kampong were heard by the same young Paris musicians that June. Rimsky was on a podium with an orchestra. The Javanese musicians were part of a display and are known almost entirely through listeners like Tiersot and, later, Debussy.

convergences.label: The tower judged by writers and a painter
convergences.note: Within three days Goncourt dined on the tower and Gauguin praised its iron. Goncourt took notes on the lift and the sunset, while Gauguin saw a new decorative art. Maupassant, who had signed against it, was already planning to get away from it.

convergences.label: Living people in the picture weeklies
convergences.note: Through August and September the illustrated papers printed the Kanak, Senegalese and Annamese villages week after week, and the Paris press covered the Lakota at Neuilly. The people shown are named almost nowhere, except a few Javanese dancers and Red Shirt.

convergences.label: Lunch on the tower
convergences.note: The inventor, the engineer and Gounod, one of the 1887 protesters, ate together on the first platform. Edison's dedication praised Eiffel as a builder. The protest of two and a half years earlier was not mentioned in any surviving record of the day.

convergences.label: Going home
convergences.note: When the fair closed, the tower stayed and the displays were taken down. The Javanese travelled home by Genoa with medals showing the tower. The people of the colonial villages leave almost no trace after the illustrated weeklies stop printing them.

ties.note: Maupassant signed the 1887 protest that Eiffel answered in print. In 1890 he wrote that the finished tower had helped drive him out of Paris.
Edison lunched on the tower and visited Eiffel's rooms at the top on 10 September 1889, giving him a phonograph and an English dedication.
Goncourt dined on Eiffel's tower in July 1889 and described its lifts and stairs in the Journal.
Brothers. Theo's letters were Vincent's main window on the Exposition.
Married in Amsterdam on 17 April 1889, three weeks before the fair opened.
Sister-in-law. She later edited and published Vincent's letters, including those about 1889.
Theo was Gauguin's dealer. He turned down Gauguin's plan to hang six of Vincent's pictures at the Café des Arts.
They had shared the Yellow House in Arles until December 1888. In June 1889 Vincent read the announcement of Gauguin's café show from the asylum.
Debussy heard the kampong's gamelan. That it shaped his later music is his own later claim and a widely held position among scholars.
Tiersot transcribed the kampong's music and named a dancer, Tamina, and a performer, Rimbo.
Both men listened at the kampong in the same months. Tiersot published at once, while Debussy wrote of it only years later.
Gauguin visited the Javanese village and urged Bernard to see the dances. Scholars connect his later borrowings from Javanese art, including the Borobudur reliefs, to these months.

Both were living displays, and both are recorded almost entirely by others. The kampong was privately organised by a Dutch committee; the colonial villages were run by the French Ministry of the Colonies.
Both were American attractions in Paris in 1889. In 1894 Edison's studio filmed Annie Oakley shooting.

threads_out.note: Goncourt kept his Journal through both chapters. The painters at the Café des Arts called themselves the 'Impressionist and Synthetist' group, borrowing the name from the 1874 show to claim its independence, and Gauguin had exhibited with the Impressionists from 1879 to 1886.

Debussy's essay praising Javanese music appeared in early 1913, months before he sat in the audience at the premiere of The Rite of Spring. Its composer, Stravinsky, was Rimsky-Korsakov's pupil, and Ravel, said to have heard Rimsky's 1889 concerts, was also at the premiere.

The colonial villages of 1889 and the objects taken from Benin City in 1897 were both shown in European capitals by the powers that ruled their makers. In both cases the people concerned appear mainly in the records of those who displayed them.

The Benz Patent-Motorwagen, a three-wheeled petrol car first driven in 1886, was shown at the 1889 Paris Exposition, sold in France by Émile Roger. It drew far less attention than the tower or the Galerie des Machines.
The Exposition was timed for the centenary of 1789 and opened on the anniversary of the Estates-General. Several European monarchies stayed away officially for that reason.
